notes.definition: The glucose made in photosynthesis is used by the plant for respiration, converted into starch, fats and oils for storage, used to make cellulose for cell walls, and used with nitrate ions to make amino acids for protein synthesis.
explanation: Photosynthesis makes glucose, but a plant cannot simply keep all of it as glucose. Instead, the glucose is used in five main ways: for respiration, to make starch for storage, to make fats or oils for storage, to make cellulose for cell walls, and to make amino acids, which are then built into proteins.

Respiration: some glucose is used in respiration in every living plant cell, day and night. Respiration transfers the energy the plant needs for living processes, such as building larger molecules, active transport of mineral ions into root hair cells, and cell division for growth.

Storage as starch: glucose is converted into starch, which is insoluble. This makes it a good storage molecule because it does not dissolve, so it does not affect the movement of water into and out of cells by osmosis, and it stays where it is stored. Starch is stored in leaves (in chloroplasts) and in storage organs such as potato tubers. When the plant needs energy, for example at night, starch is broken back down into glucose for respiration.

Storage as fats and oils: glucose can also be converted into fats or oils, which are especially common as energy stores in seeds such as sunflower seeds, peanuts and rapeseed. Fats and oils are insoluble in water too.

Cellulose: glucose is used to make cellulose, which strengthens the cell wall. Growing parts of a plant, such as shoot tips, need lots of cellulose for the walls of new cells. Amino acids and proteins: glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but proteins also contain nitrogen. So plants combine sugars from glucose with nitrate ions and other mineral ions absorbed from the soil to make amino acids. The amino acids are joined together to make proteins, such as enzymes.
keyFacts: Glucose is used for respiration, which transfers energy for living processes.
Glucose is converted into insoluble starch for storage.
Glucose is converted into fats or oils for storage, especially in seeds.
Glucose is used to make cellulose, which strengthens the cell wall.
Glucose is used to make amino acids for protein synthesis.
To make amino acids, plants combine sugars with nitrate ions and other mineral ions absorbed from the soil.
Starch is a good store because it is insoluble, so it does not affect osmosis.
Stored starch is converted back to glucose when the plant needs energy, for example at night.
Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present.

keyTerms.definition: An insoluble carbohydrate made from glucose; used by plants as an energy store.
A carbohydrate made from glucose that strengthens plant cell walls.
Small molecules that join together to make proteins; plants make them from sugars and nitrate ions.
Mineral ions absorbed from the soil by root hair cells; they supply the nitrogen needed to make amino acids.
Does not dissolve in water, so it does not affect the movement of water by osmosis.
Insoluble energy stores made from glucose, common in seeds.

workedExamples.title: Why starch, not glucose, is stored
workedExamples.question: Explain why a potato tuber stores starch rather than glucose.
steps: Identify the property: starch is insoluble; glucose is soluble.
Explain the problem with glucose: dissolved glucose would draw water into the cells by osmosis and could move out of the cells.
Conclude: starch can be stored in large amounts without affecting water movement and stays in the storage cells.
workedExamples.answer: Starch is insoluble, so it does not affect the movement of water by osmosis and stays in the cells; glucose is soluble and would.

workedExamples.title: Making proteins from glucose
workedExamples.question: Describe how a plant uses glucose to make proteins.
steps: Glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so another element (nitrogen) is needed.
Root hair cells absorb nitrate ions (and other mineral ions) from the soil.
Sugars from glucose are combined with the nitrate ions to make amino acids.
The amino acids are joined together to make proteins, for example enzymes.
workedExamples.answer: Glucose is combined with nitrate ions from the soil to make amino acids, which are then joined to make proteins.

workedExamples.title: Matching uses to plant parts
workedExamples.question: Suggest the main use of glucose in (a) a sunflower seed and (b) a growing shoot tip.
steps: (a) Seeds need an energy store for when they germinate. Sunflower seeds are oily, so the glucose has been converted to oil for storage.
(b) A shoot tip is making many new cells. Each new cell needs a cell wall, so glucose is used to make cellulose; it is also used for respiration and to make amino acids for proteins.
workedExamples.answer: (a) Stored as oil. (b) Making cellulose for new cell walls (plus respiration and proteins).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants store glucose as glucose.
misconceptions.right: In fact plants convert most stored glucose into insoluble starch (or fats and oils), because soluble glucose would affect the movement of water by osmosis.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants can make proteins from glucose alone.
misconceptions.right: In fact proteins contain nitrogen, which glucose does not. Plants must combine sugars with nitrate ions from the soil to make amino acids first.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants only use glucose for energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact glucose is also the raw material for building cellulose, starch, fats, oils and proteins, which make up most of the plant's biomass.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants get nitrate ions from the air.
misconceptions.right: In fact nitrate ions are absorbed from the soil by root hair cells, along with other mineral ions.

realWorld: Potatoes, rice and wheat are staple foods because these plants store large amounts of starch made from glucose.
Vegetable oils such as sunflower oil and rapeseed oil come from seeds, where plants store glucose as oil.
Farmers add nitrate fertilisers to soil so that crops can make enough amino acids and proteins to grow well.
Cotton and paper are made mostly of cellulose, which plants make from glucose for their cell walls.
examTips: Learn the five uses as a list: respiration, starch, fats/oils, cellulose, amino acids for proteins. Exam questions often ask for two or three.
When explaining why starch is stored, use the word 'insoluble' and link it to osmosis.
For protein synthesis, always mention nitrate ions from the soil. Saying 'nitrogen from the air' does not get the mark.
Say cellulose 'strengthens the cell wall', not just 'makes the cell wall'.
summary: Glucose is used for respiration to transfer energy.
It is converted into insoluble starch for storage.
It is converted into fats or oils for storage, especially in seeds.
It is used to make cellulose, which strengthens cell walls.
With nitrate ions from the soil, it is used to make amino acids, which form proteins.
Starch is a good store because it is insoluble and does not affect osmosis.

flashcards.front: What do plants combine with sugars to make amino acids?

flashcards.front: What are amino acids used to make?

flashcards.back: In seeds (for example sunflower seeds and peanuts).

flashcards.front: Why does a plant need glucose for respiration?

questions.question: In what form do plants such as potatoes store glucose?
markScheme: 1 mark: starch
questions.explanation: Potato tubers convert glucose into insoluble starch for storage. Cellulose is used for cell walls, not storage. Proteins need nitrate ions and are not mainly a store.

questions.question: What is cellulose used for in a plant?
markScheme: 1 mark: strengthening the cell wall
questions.explanation: Cellulose is made from glucose and strengthens plant cell walls. Energy in seeds is stored as starch or oils. Chlorophyll absorbs light. Enzymes are proteins made from amino acids.

questions.question: Which mineral ions do plants combine with sugars to make amino acids?
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrate ions
questions.explanation: Amino acids contain nitrogen. Plants get nitrogen as nitrate ions absorbed from the soil. The other ions do not supply nitrogen.

questions.question: Which property of starch makes it a good storage molecule?
markScheme: 1 mark: it is insoluble in water
questions.explanation: Because starch is insoluble, it does not affect the movement of water by osmosis and stays in the cells. A substance that dissolves easily, like glucose, would cause water to move into the cells. Starch does not contain nitrogen.

questions.question: Where do plants get the nitrate ions they need to make amino acids?
options: From carbon dioxide in the air
From the soil, through root hair cells
From oxygen produced in the leaves
markScheme: 1 mark: from the soil, through root hair cells
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions are mineral ions dissolved in soil water and absorbed by root hair cells. Glucose, carbon dioxide and oxygen contain no nitrogen.

questions.question: Sunflower seeds contain a large energy store made from glucose. What is this store mainly made of?
markScheme: 1 mark: oil
questions.explanation: Many seeds, including sunflower seeds, store glucose as oil, which is why sunflower oil can be extracted from them. Cellulose is structural, amino acids are used for proteins and chlorophyll is a pigment.

questions.question: Plants use amino acids to make which type of substance?
markScheme: 1 mark: proteins
questions.explanation: Amino acids are joined together to make proteins such as enzymes. Starch and cellulose are made from glucose, and fats are made from glucose too, not from amino acids.

questions.question: Why do plant cells use some of their glucose in respiration?
options: To transfer energy for living processes
markScheme: 1 mark: to transfer energy for living processes
questions.explanation: Respiration transfers energy from glucose for processes such as building larger molecules and active transport. Respiration uses oxygen rather than making it, and storing glucose as starch is a different use.

questions.question: Some plants store energy in their seeds as oil rather than starch. Which is the most likely advantage of this?
options: Oil is soluble so it moves easily around the seed
Oil stores more energy in a smaller mass, so seeds can be lighter
Oil contains nitrogen for making proteins
Oil can be used to make cellulose directly
markScheme: 1 mark: oil stores more energy in a smaller mass, so seeds can be lighter
questions.explanation: Fats and oils store about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates, so seeds can be small and light, which helps dispersal. Oils are insoluble, not soluble, and they contain no nitrogen.

questions.question: Glucose is soluble. What would most likely happen if a plant cell stored large amounts of glucose instead of starch?
options: Extra water would move into the cell by osmosis, upsetting its water balance
The glucose would be denatured by enzymes
Water would leave the cell by osmosis, making it more turgid
markScheme: 1 mark: extra water would move into the cell by osmosis, upsetting its water balance
questions.explanation: Dissolved glucose makes the cell contents more concentrated, so water moves in by osmosis. Water leaving a cell would make it less turgid (flaccid), not more. Only proteins such as enzymes can be denatured.

questions.question: A seed germinates underground in the dark. What is the main use of its stored starch before its first leaves reach the light?
options: Converting it back into glucose for respiration and growth
Keeping it as starch to absorb water
Releasing it into the soil as food for the roots
markScheme: 1 mark: converting it back into glucose for respiration and growth
questions.explanation: In the dark the seedling cannot photosynthesise, so it breaks down stored starch into glucose. This is used in respiration to transfer energy and to make new cell walls and proteins for growth.

questions.question: Which of these substances is NOT made from glucose by plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrate ions
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions are mineral ions taken in from the soil; they are not made by the plant. Starch, cellulose and oils are all made from glucose.

questions.question: A plant is grown with plenty of light, water and carbon dioxide, but in soil with no nitrate ions. Which substance will it be least able to make?
markScheme: 1 mark: proteins
questions.explanation: Without nitrate ions the plant cannot make amino acids, so it cannot make proteins. Starch, cellulose and fats contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, all of which come from photosynthesis.

questions.question: Give three ways in which plants use the glucose made in photosynthesis.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three from: respiration; converted to starch for storage; converted to fats or oils for storage; to make cellulose to strengthen cell walls; to make amino acids for protein synthesis
questions.explanation: There are five uses to learn. Make each answer specific: for example 'to make cellulose for cell walls' rather than just 'to grow'.

questions.question: Name the substance made from glucose that strengthens plant cell walls.
markScheme: 1 mark: cellulose
questions.explanation: Cellulose is the main component of plant cell walls. Do not confuse it with cell membrane or with starch, which is a storage molecule.

questions.question: Explain why plants convert glucose into starch for storage.
markScheme: 1 mark: starch is insoluble
1 mark: so it does not affect the movement of water into or out of cells by osmosis / it stays in the storage cells
questions.explanation: Glucose is soluble and would cause water to move into cells by osmosis. Starch is insoluble, so large amounts can be stored safely.

questions.question: Describe how plants use glucose to make proteins.
markScheme: 1 mark: sugars from glucose are combined with nitrate ions (from the soil) to make amino acids
1 mark: amino acids are joined together to make proteins
questions.explanation: Proteins are chains of amino acids. Amino acids need nitrogen, so plants combine sugars with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil.

questions.question: Plant cells use glucose in respiration. Give two processes in a plant that need the energy transferred by respiration.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: building larger molecules (e.g. proteins, cellulose, starch); active transport of mineral ions into root hair cells; cell division / growth
questions.explanation: Energy from respiration is needed for building large molecules from small ones and for active transport. Plants do not need energy for movement of the whole body or for keeping warm in the way animals do.

questions.question: Name one type of energy store, other than starch, that plants make from glucose.
markScheme: 1 mark: fats or oils
questions.explanation: Plants store glucose as starch, fats or oils. Fats and oils are especially common in seeds.

questions.question: Name the mineral ion that plants need to make amino acids.
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrate (ions)
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions supply the nitrogen needed in amino acids. 'Nitrogen' alone is not enough, because plants cannot use nitrogen gas from the air.

questions.question: The tip of a growing shoot is producing new cells very quickly. Suggest and explain why it needs a large supply of glucose.
markScheme: 1 mark: to make cellulose for the cell walls of new cells
1 mark: to make amino acids / proteins for new cells (e.g. enzymes, membranes)
1 mark: for respiration to transfer energy for cell division / building large molecules
questions.explanation: Every new cell needs a cellulose wall and proteins, and making them uses energy from respiration. So glucose is needed both as a building material and as a fuel.

questions.question: Plants cannot photosynthesise at night, but their cells still respire. Explain how plant cells get glucose for respiration at night.
markScheme: 1 mark: starch stored during the day (in leaves or storage organs)
1 mark: is broken down / converted back into glucose for respiration
questions.explanation: During the day, excess glucose is stored as insoluble starch. At night, the starch is broken back down to glucose, which is used in respiration.

questions.question: A leaf was kept in bright light for 6 hours and then tested with iodine solution. Describe the result you would expect and explain what it shows about the use of glucose.
markScheme: 1 mark: the iodine turns (from orange-brown to) blue-black
1 mark: shows starch is present, so glucose made in photosynthesis has been converted to starch for storage
questions.explanation: Starch is not made directly by photosynthesis. Its presence shows glucose was made and then converted into starch. The blue-black colour is the positive test.

questions.question: Starch and cellulose are both made from glucose. Give one difference between how plants use starch and how they use cellulose.
markScheme: 1 mark: starch is used as an energy store
1 mark: cellulose is used to strengthen cell walls
questions.explanation: Both are made by joining glucose molecules, but starch is broken down again for energy when needed, while cellulose stays in the cell wall as a structural material.

questions.question: Explain why a plant cannot make proteins using only the glucose from photosynthesis.
markScheme: 1 mark: glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen / no nitrogen
1 mark: amino acids (and proteins) contain nitrogen, so nitrate ions from the soil are needed
questions.explanation: All the elements in glucose come from carbon dioxide and water. Proteins also need nitrogen, which comes from nitrate ions in the soil.

questions.question: Describe the different ways in which a plant uses the glucose it makes in photosynthesis.
markScheme: Indicative content: used in respiration to transfer energy; converted to insoluble starch for storage (e.g. in potato tubers, leaves); converted to fats or oils for storage (e.g. in seeds); used to make cellulose to strengthen cell walls; combined with nitrate ions from the soil to make amino acids; amino acids used to make proteins.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes at least four uses clearly, with detail such as the purpose of each or the need for nitrate ions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or two uses with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A full answer covers all five uses and adds a purpose to each one, for example 'cellulose strengthens the cell wall'. Mentioning nitrate ions for amino acids shows depth.

questions.question: A bean plant grows a new leaf. Explain how the plant uses glucose from photosynthesis, together with substances absorbed from the soil, to build the new leaf and to store energy for later.
markScheme: Indicative content: glucose made in photosynthesis in existing leaves; some used in respiration to transfer energy for building larger molecules and cell division; glucose converted to cellulose to make and strengthen cell walls of new cells; sugars combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil by root hair cells to make amino acids; amino acids joined to make proteins (e.g. enzymes for the new cells); other mineral ions from the soil also used; excess glucose converted to insoluble starch for storage (does not affect osmosis); some stored as fats or oils, e.g. in bean seeds; stored starch broken down to glucose when needed (e.g. at night).

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and coherent explanation covering building materials (cellulose, proteins with nitrate ions), energy from respiration, and storage as starch and/or oils with reasons.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains several uses of glucose with some links to building the leaf or storage, but with some gaps, e.g. nitrate ions or reasons for storage missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): lists simple uses of glucose with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The best answers separate glucose's two roles: a source of energy (respiration) and a raw material (cellulose, amino acids, starch, oils). They link the soil to nitrate ions for amino acids and explain why starch is an effective store.
